utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Could you call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam. All the accused are here. I notice from the defence teams, the absence of Mr. Krgovic. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He'll be working away from the courtroom for a few days, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Long cross-examinations on the horizon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's our forte, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. The witness is already in the courtroom. Just one thing before we proceed. We're sitting pursuant to Rule 15(a) for the first part of today's sitting. Judge Stole will join us after the first break. So good afternoon to you, witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremic, can you hear me? Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, and welcome back. We hope to finish with your testimony within the next half an hour, I suppose, and then you're free to go home, and I thank you for bearing with us. Mr. Sarapa, you were still in possession of the floor yesterday when we adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not working?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is your working, Mr. Haynes? It's working now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Sarapa, and I thank the technicians. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Jeremic, once again. Just a few more questions, without using any documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: You were told to write an order concerning the punishment of Djokic, father and son. In that connection, did Vinko Pandurevic ever address you?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Do you recall if you wrote that order, in fact?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Do you then allow the possibility that you did not write it?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Have you ever seen the order to punish Djokic father and son signed by Vinko Pandurevic or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning the father and son Djokic, I don't remember seeing an order in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And my last question: If one takes into account that a criminal act was involved in this case, that a decision to remand these people in custody was taken, which is pre-criminal trial action, that it was addressed to the military prosecutor's office and that you never saw that order, does the possibility exist or is it a possibility that the order was never written?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you very much, and I wish you a safe trip home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Sarapa. Ms. Nikolic, yesterday I got the impression from you that in the wake of the Pandurevic cross-examination, you wished to put some further questions to the witness; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. With the Chamber's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Is there an opposition on the part of the Prosecution, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It's a little unusual, but we are unusual ourselves sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it's an unusual --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We've got no objection to the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's an unusual setup, and he was asked questions and he answered questions relating to the accused Nikolic. After that, the Nikolic Defence had concluded their cross-examination, so I think the opportunity should be given, and we'll carry out from there and we'll see how to regulate the proceedings after this. Yes, Ms. Nikolic. Yes, Mr. Pandurevic, I see you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I was simply going to say that Ms. Nikolic and I have spoken about this, and in the circumstances I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremic, good afternoon again.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I will do my best to be very brief in my examination today. I just want certain clarifications on points that remained unclear after your testimony yesterday in response to the questions by Mr. Sarapa. When pronouncing disciplinary measures such as military detention, such measures could be decided on only by the commander or deputy commander; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If military detention is involved, the measures were decided on by battalion commanders, and it was the brigade commander who decided on military imprisonment. I don't remember the brigade commander deciding on military detention or remand in custody.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And that could be 20 to 60 days, depending on the criminal act involved?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the minimal sentence, but I know we wrote orders involving up to 60 days of military prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic and Mr. Jeremic, please allow a short pause between question and answer, because the interpreters are really trying hard to catch up with you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Criminal reports and drafting of other documents, documents involved in criminal proceedings and those necessary for the military prosecutor's office were the responsibility of your service and the chief of security, Drago Nikolic, was responsible for compiling such documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Other documents that your service for crime prevention drafted, such as records on crime scene investigation, witness statements, records on identification, would be signed by you or other clerks in the service for crime prevention.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown just one document prescribing military prison, 3D123. We have a draft in English made by our team, but we haven't got the official translation yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremic, I'm sorry, your answer to my previous question concerning other documents written by your service, records of crime scene investigation, records of identification, the taking of statements, et cetera, would be signed by you, as the official -- as the authorised officer, or clerks in the service?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I, too, was a clerk in that service.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, but your answer is not recorded.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All these concerns also include sketches made by the civilian police and the photo documentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Look at the document now on the screen. Is this the format that you followed? Look at the heading. Could we scroll the document to see the bottom, please. Is this the type of document your service drafted?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say with certainty whether it is one of ours. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: But it looks like the format that you used?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Scroll it back up, please. It was a long time ago. I cannot give you an answer with absolute certainty either way, and I am not familiar with this name here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That was January 1994 or 1995. The year is not clear. Maybe you didn't draft it at all.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I was absent then.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Maybe it was written by somebody else in your service?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anything is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Nikolic. Is there re-examination, Mr. Thayer? Yesterday, you said you had a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I stated I had three questions. And with the leave of the Court and consent of my friends, I'd ask to reopen my redirect just to ask this witness what his age was. I typically ask our witnesses how old they are, and I failed to do that. And if -- if there's consent from my friends and leave of the Court, I'd just like to ask the witness what his age is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I thank the Court and my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, could you just tell the Court how old you are, please?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fifty-two.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I just have two questions for you, sir. You testified yesterday about a 24-hour period of time where you were assigned to guard the gate at Standard; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You also recall an occasion when some of your colleagues were sent to Orahovac to guard prisoners at the school there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know then who was going to Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The -- my question is, though: Do you recall an occasion when some of your colleagues were sent to the school at Grbavci to guard some prisoners, whether you remember their names or not?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really didn't know where they were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. But at some point, did you become aware that some of your colleagues had been sent to guard prisoners at the Grbavci school?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned I don't know how much later after that guard duty at the gate. It could be five, ten, or fifteen days. I said as much yesterday. There was stories making the rounds within the barracks as to what happened, what had happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So my only question on this topic, sir, is: Do you recall whether you were on this 24-hour guard duty at the same time that your colleagues were guarding prisoners in Orahovac or was this a different time? That's my only question on that issue.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, almost the entire military police company was absent. Where they were, I really don't know, and that's when I stayed at the gate, and that is why I stood at the gate in the first place, because otherwise I never stood guard at the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, did the military prosecutor's office have a representative stationed with your crime prevention service unit or detailed to your unit?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any recollection of any representative from the military prosecutor's office ever being stationed with your unit or detailed to your unit?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So my last question, sir, is: In your experience, how would the military prosecutor's office or a military court become informed of a potential criminal offence being committed by a Zvornik Brigade soldier?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that our service, the one I worked in, notified the military prosecutor's office of any criminal acts in the form of criminal reports. Whether anybody else reported such things to the military prosecutor's office, I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Judge Kwon, Judge Prost. Mr. Jeremic, there are no further questions for you, which means your testimony finishes here, and our staff will assist you. You're free to go home, and before you leave the courtroom, I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony, and also on behalf of everyone, wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Documents, exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has distributed its tender sheet. We would offer the exhibits listed thereon, with the exception of numbers 387 and 388. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You don't have it. Then I'll just read the 65 ter numbers, then. Okay. And we'll be working off the exhibit list, then, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we're looking at the exhibit list for this witness, the Prosecution would tender the entire list, with the exception of 65 ter numbers 387 and 388.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So essentially we're talking of 385 -- 65 ter numbers 385, 386, 389, 390, 391, 392, 393, 394; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And all these documents have corresponding translation into English?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Indeed they do, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections on the part of any of the Defence teams? We hear none, so these documents are being admitted. Now we come to Defence documents. Mr. Zivanovic, do you have any documents you would like to tender? Ms. Nikolic? Mr. Meek, I don't suppose you have, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have two documents to tender, 3D122, that's the sketch that the witness drew during proofing, and 123, the one that was shown to the witness today, 3D123.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this last document, you said, has been translated by yourselves? We do not have an official translation of it?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It's a provisional translation to use today. But as soon as the official one is available, we will tender it. This was just a temporary thing to enable us to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection on the part of the Prosecution or any of the Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: None, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I hear no objections from the other Defence teams, so 3D122 is admitted, 3D123 will be marked for identification pending an official translation thereof, upon which it will automatically be introduced in the list of admitted documents. Okay. Ms. Nikolic -- sorry. I was going to refer you to the corrections that you wanted to make to the -- to yesterday's transcript, but perhaps I will ask Mr. Sarapa first if he has any documents to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those are the documents that exist in B/C/S and in English, formation 7D361, 7D370, and P385. To be marked for identification, since we haven't got the translation yet, we tender 7D356, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So as I -- if I understood you, well, the one that is still not yet translated is this last one, 7D356; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's a document that -- for which translation is pending. It's the only one that hasn't been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. My attention is being drawn at P385 has already been admitted as a Prosecution document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, as has 7D361 as well under a different "P" number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you not use 7D311?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I don't want to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer, what is the corresponding exhibit number for 7D361?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm looking at that right now, Your Honour. That is -- with the Court's indulgence --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's P407, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In view of that, do you wish to introduce it, Mr. Sarapa, nonetheless as your document? I don't think there is a need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, there is no need to have it admitted as our document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That leaves us with 7D370. Any objection, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: None, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any of the other Defence teams, any objection? None. It is so admitted. 7D356, any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: None, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any other -- or any objection from any other Defence teams? None. So this will be marked for identification, pending translation, upon the same terms as usual. All right. Thank you. I think we can now move to Ms. Nikolic once more. Yesterday, before we adjourned, Ms. Nikolic, you said that you had noticed several mistakes in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. One error has been removed in the edited version, in the revised version of the transcript, and the others have been listed in paper that we sent to the legal officer, so I don't believe we need spend more time on it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Very kind of you, Ms. Nikolic. Thank you. Mr. Thayer, will you be in charge of the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. McCloskey will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Can we proceed? So let's bring the next witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we just hold off for just one second? I just wanted to alert the Court to just small issues. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go into private session just for a second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll see if any specific request is made by the witness, in which case we will hear submissions. Okay. I think you may proceed to escort the witness in the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's never given evidence before, has he?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Galic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to welcome you. You're about to start your testimony. Before you do so, our rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. The text you already have in your hands. Please read it out loud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us, that you will be speaking the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I ask you to make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have a seat, please. The procedure here is like in most criminal courts. The Prosecution, Mr. McCloskey, will be putting some questions to you, and he will then be followed by some of the Defence teams on cross-examination. I don't expect your testimony to finish today, but we'll try and do our best. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Galic.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you first begin by spelling your name for us? Tell us your full name and spell your last.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Mihajlo Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you spell the last just so we get it right in the record?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: G-a-l-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when were you born?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 13th of February, 1951.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I was born in Celopek, Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I grew up in Celopek and Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you give us a brief outline of your educational background?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I completed elementary school and the secondary teachers college, and then I started working. And while working, I graduated from the higher school of economics. That's as far as my education is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did you graduate from the economics school with that degree?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I completed this school of economics in 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you do professionally after that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I worked as a teacher in the elementary school in Zvornik, and then in the municipality authorities of Zvornik, and then again in the elementary school in Zvornik. And after the war, after 1996, between the 22nd of April, 1996, and the 1st of August, 1998, I worked in the transportation company called Drinatrans. And from the 1st of August of 1998 until the 22nd of March, 2004, I have been a professional soldier in the army of Republika Srpska. And then is when my years of service ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And right now are you working at all or are you retired?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I'm not working. I'm retired. I have been retired since the 22nd of March, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us an outline of your military career? We just saw the end of it. Can you start at the beginning, perhaps if you did JNA service, and perhaps give us an outline of that? Why don't we -- leading up to 1995, if you could.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I did my military service in 1971 to 1972 in the school for officers in reserve in Zadar, and I have the status of an officer in reserve. From 1992 until the end of 1996, I was mobilised and I was in the regional headquarters in the battalion, in the brigade command, and that is where my activities in the military ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Tell us about your position in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I was assistant chief of staff for personnel affairs and mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's in the command of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was your immediate supervisor or superior, excuse me, in that position?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: My immediate superior was the Chief of Staff, Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us what your duties and responsibilities were in that job at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: The activities of the personnel service that I headed were as follows: Replenishment of units with manpower, materiel; then all other activities related to cooperation with the Defence ministry department which was responsible for replenishment of unit materiel; keeping of records for all military conscripts, officers and non-commissioned officers and privates; also activities in relation to dealing with all personnel issues of members of the unit; keeping all possible records in the unit for the missing, the wounded, the killed; also participation in the work of various-level medical commissions, monitoring the state of health of the wounded who were undergoing treatment; issuance of various certificates about wounds suffered or deaths and other certificates on the participation of soldiers in the units. Those would briefly be the activities that the personnel service engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what rank did you hold in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: In July 1995, I had the rank of major.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what rank did you hold in '92, when you were first mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I was captain first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so who promoted you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: The Defence ministry or the main staff. I can't remember exactly what the order said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And your commander at the time was Vinko Pandurevic, of your promotion?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How many people, if any, did you supervise in your job in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: There was only another officer working with me in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was his name?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Andjelko Ivanovic. Unfortunately, he is deceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I want to take you to the 13th of July, 1995, something I know you've talked to the ICTY about. Can you tell us, sometime during that day did you get a certain assignment, something that was a bit out of the ordinary?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, in the evening, about 2200 or 2300 hours, I was already resting by then, I was tasked to go to the forward command post in Kitovnice to replace Lieutenant Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were you when you first heard about your replacement for Lieutenant Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I was in the brigade headquarters, and as it was the evening, I was resting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how, in particular, as you recall, did you find out about this job?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I can't say with certainty, but I think it was the courier, the messenger, who came and conveyed the message to me. I got ready, and with a vehicle and a driver, I went up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the driver that took you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember. One of the drivers on duty, but I really can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So was this a regularly-scheduled position for you or was there something unusual about this date and time?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I was to be on duty on the 14th in the morning, starting with 7.00 a.m. We were usually on duty for 24 hours, but on the 13th, this was an extraordinary shift duty, and I took over duty up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You said it was duty at the forward command post, and you've told us where that is. Can you describe a little bit what the duties and responsibilities of the duty officer at the forward command post are?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: If I can recall correctly, it is to monitor the situation along the defence line, to observe, and if it is possible, to carry out observation depending on the light, whether it's daytime or night-time, contacts with units and, in other words, monitors the overall situation along the separation line. That is the basic duty of an officer at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What sorts of people were assigned to that post? Could it have been anybody in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No, only officers, commanding officers in the brigade, according to an established schedule for a certain period. Now, whether those schedules were fortnightly or monthly, I can't recall, but they were commanding officers from the brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know why it was limited to officers?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember anything in particular to give you as an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was it an important job?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes, one of the more important activities of the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How far away from the IKM were the enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: From the IKM and their observation post, it may be 1.000 or 1.500 metres. That would be the closest line. To the right and left, the distance is normally greater, but it is very close so that one can monitor the situation. At least the area that one can observe visually, whereas everything else is monitored through the communication means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me take you back to that evening when you were driving to the forward command post. Can you just roughly describe what route you took?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: The customary route, Karakaj-Jardan-Kitovnice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you got to the forward command post, what did you find?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, a soldier was there working with the communications and a soldier -- another soldier who was the messenger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember their names?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember the names of either one of them because this was, after all, a long time ago and I don't have those names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was the man you were to replace there Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you speak to him?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I didn't speak to Drago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see him?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do you know he was there?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the schedule that was in the unit, and I was told to go and replace him. His name was given to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. But this is -- can you describe the forward command post, the kind of building it is, the size of the facility itself?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: The forward command post was a small building, a holiday home of prefabricated type, with two premises, as far as I can recollect. It was in the area of Kitovnice, and the observation post was some 500 or more metres away, closer to the separation line, and this was also part of the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So are you -- now, when I ask you if Drago Nikolic was there at the time, do you remember what you told us in your interview about that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't find him then, nor did I talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. There may have been some confusion, I'm not sure, but earlier when I asked you if he was there, I thought you said he was. So just to try to clarify it, when you got to the forward command post that night, do you -- was Drago Nikolic there?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: When I got there, he wasn't there. Before that, I assume he was, but I didn't find him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you replace someone in a situation like this, should they be there before the person arrives to replace them?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: He should be there, according to the rules. Now, why we didn't meet there, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ask or did anybody tell you where he went, what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How long did you have duty there up at the forward command post? From that night, that is.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Until the 15th, in the morning, at 7.00 a.m., when the next officer came to replace me according to schedule and to take over those duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember who replaced you on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: As there was nothing in the notebook, I don't know whether it's the right thing to say, but I think it was Major Ljubo Bojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You may remember me telling you you're not supposed to speculate, but if you believe something, you can say if you think it's true. Do you think you're speculating or do you think it's something you have some confidence in?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I believe it was him because on that day he wrote certain documents at that place, and I gave this matter some thought and came to the conclusion that he was the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll get to a document or two on that subject. Is Mr. Bojanovic still alive today?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, not. He died a month or so ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if I could, I want to show you what you have seen before. It's a copy of the IKM logbook, 65 ter 347.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could get the English and the B/C/S up there, if possible. And the B/C/S, the part I'm looking for is on page 8, and in the English it's on page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that sometimes takes a while, but is this something that was shown to you by an investigator some time ago, and then most recently in my office a day or two ago?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And take a look at the screen in front of you. Were you able to see the original in my office?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you've had a little time to look at it and concentrate for a while, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So tell us what this is, as you look on this picture and see this handwriting and this date, 13/7/95. Is that -- are those entries of the logbook?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about the logbook, what it is, what it was designed to do?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: The purpose of this diary, of this logbook, was to record -- to enter all activities reported or notified by the duty officer at the forward command post, the situation at the separation line and other indicators of the situation on the ground. That's the main thing that should be entered and that is recorded in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recognise the handwriting for this -- this 13 July entry?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And whose handwriting is that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that your --

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Although you can't see the signature there, not yet, but, yes, I did sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then can we bring it up a little bit so we can find the area that ... Okay. I don't need the top -- those top paragraphs, just the "13 July," please. And I just noted in the English translation it says "Major Talic." That's an error, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You didn't put your name as Talic? Is that an error, "Talic," or can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: It's an error. Instead of "T," a "G." But in fact -- in fact, you know about this man who was -- used to be here, had -- his last name was almost the same as mine. He came here alive and left this place dead. My name is Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right, okay. And do you know when you made that 13 July entry in the logbook?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: It was entered during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know which day, I mean, if you got there in the evening?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: At 2300 hours. That's the upper entry. And on this 14th of July, the entry refers to that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. The part that I'm asking about, and I'm sorry, I'll be more clear, is where you say, and I'll read it: "I took over duty, unscheduled, from Lieutenant Drago Nikolic at 2300 hours." Do you know when you wrote that entry?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I suppose, in fact I think, that this was written when I came up there or, rather, no, in the morning, it was in the morning, because the following entry is about how the night had passed. And then I wrote on the 14th, in the morning, based on all the information incoming to the forward command post during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, thank you. When you got there and didn't find Drago Nikolic, did you contact him or attempt to contact him in any way to find out what happened to him or get an update on what had happened while he was there?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No, I did not try to contact him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see the last entry, I believe it's -- can we bring the English down a little bit so I can see perhaps the date? The other way. All right. We see the last entry in the book at 1820 hours, so we have between 1820 hours and 2300 hours on the front line. A lot can happen in that amount of time. Did you get any information of what, if anything, had been going on?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No. All that happened, to my knowledge, firsthand knowledge, and all the things that were reported to me, is reflected in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me take you to that other document I think you may have made a reference to, and that's 65 ter 347. It's a -- I'm sorry, 65 ter 329. And I think I'll give you the original again so you can look at it as well. And we'll get that up on the -- if we could get the English up as well, if we could. This is a 15 July report, and I notice you've got a chance to look at -- do you recognise that, that document you've got in your hands?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: This is an interim combat report sent on the 15th of July, 1995, to the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: This document was sent by the then-commander, Lieutenant-Colonel Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we catch the signature on the Cyrillic, please? It's down at the bottom, I believe. Oh, it's on the next page; actually on the back of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, have you seen Vinko Pandurevic's signature quite a bit?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Very often and many times, in view of the fact that he signed most documents, especially when his deputy was absent, so I am familiar with his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So is this his regular signature?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Not regular. Sometimes he used the abbreviated version of his signature, such as this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So as you look at that original squiggle, you recognise that as his abbreviated signature?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I think that's the short version of Pandurevic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise the handwriting in this document?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And whose handwriting do you recognise?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: This report was written by Major Ljubo Bojanovic. That's his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Now, I have on my list the Defence teams of Gvero, General Gvero, and Borovcanin, who do not wish to, at least for the time being, cross-examine the witness, and then I have a reduced estimate by the Pandurevic Defence team of about an hour and a half. I still have two hours, 30 minutes asked by the Nikolic team.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's the case, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then roughly an hour to be divided between the Beara, Popovic and Miletic teams. So may I suggest either the Defence for Mr. Nikolic or the Defence for Mr. Pandurevic to go first, if there is nothing against --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm perfectly willing to go first, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because we have a break, maybe we take a break now and then we continue on and stop?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We should have a break in about 4 minutes time, we might as well have it now. Twenty-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Galic.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to begin simply by confirming with you that on the 21st of September, 2001, you met with investigators from the Prosecution and that you had an interview which was taped; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I would also like to confirm with you that on the 27th of June, 2002, you had a further investigation -- sorry, a further interview that was also recorded. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall that for both interviews, you spoke with the same investigator, and his name was Dean Manning; is this something you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have quite a bit of questions for you this afternoon, and I will try to move along as swiftly as I can. And I will be, of course, using both of these interviews as a guide to move along. First, I'd like to confirm that what you mentioned to my colleague from the Prosecution, that you were a reserve officer. That was your status in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that you were demobilised, that means that you were no longer in the service, as of April of 1996?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then you were called back for service or -- as a matter of fact, you weren't called back, but you joined the service again in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So on that second occasion, you were not mobilised or drafted, you were basically given an opportunity to join back as a professional officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's when I was admitted into professional military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I take it, Mr. Galic, that you were quite happy to get back in the service in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Because I was unable to find a different line of work, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be right, Mr. Galic, in saying that the commander of the brigade at that time, Dragan Obrenovic, was instrumental in allowing you to join back the service in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: This issue is not very clear to me because it's not about Dragan Obrenovic, it's the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska that took me in. He happened to be the commander at the time, but even if it had been someone else, I would have started working again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe I will make my question more precise. Did he assist you in any way in making it possible for you to join back the service?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Looking at your description of duties, which you discussed both with my colleague earlier today as well as in your first interview, you mentioned that you had certain responsibilities, one of which was the replenishment of unit for both personnel and materiel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that if there was someone in Zvornik Brigade in 1995 who had a link with the Ministry of Defence, that was yourself?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: For the Zvornik Brigade, yes, it was me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And your task, as responsible for replenishment during wartime, was a very important duty, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: It was a very important duty, but you have to understand that for the whole duration of the war I did not perform that job that you're talking about now. I did it for a short while.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if there was a need to replenish the brigade or if there was some kind of mobilisation in the area of Zvornik, this is something you would be responsible for, along with the Ministry of Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Those who are mobilised needed for the Zvornik Brigade with the necessary permissions were my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, we spoke with some people who -- whom you might know, and I'd like to basically get your views on a couple of issues which we have gathered during the Defence investigation. And in this respect, I would like to begin by asking you whether you know someone called Branko Avramovic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you tell me what Branko Avramovic was doing in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: He was clerk for general affairs in the 3rd Infantry Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What I would like to ask of you is based on some information that I've gathered from Mr. Avramovic concerning the procedures of recruitment; that the role of the personnel officer was to be present whenever there was recruitment or new people coming in to the unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, then, can you explain?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: In matters of recruitment, a commission was established for recruitment, and that job involved the assessment of the health of the recruit, his general condition, and there was one NCO on behalf of the Zvornik Brigade who was part of that commission. But in 1994, 1995 and 1996, I don't remember the earlier years, that's the way it was. The Ministry of Defence was in charge of recruitment. What the brigade did in that period, its part of the job was to submit certain requests to the ministry, specifying the military specialisations that the unit requires so that young men would be recruited to the appropriate branches of service and later integrated into the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, what I would like to establish with you, Mr. Galic, is that if there was mobilisation, would I be right in saying that the personnel officer from the brigade command, along with the chief of personnel and a clerk from the Ministry of Defence, would be the ones to receive the recruits? Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No. Recruits were received and sent for military service by the Ministry of Defence, and the brigade did not have any jurisdiction or responsibilities in the matter, neither the brigade nor its command, except in cases when the brigade would be required to provide an assembly point where the recruits would gather and from where they would be transported to recruitment centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Galic, on 14th and 15th of July, 1995, was the Zvornik Brigade not tasked to provide a gathering area for a mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, because on the 14th I was absent, and in fact some recruits were sent to the army on that day, on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: There's another individual I'd like you to -- to ask you about to see if you know the person, and that person is -- sorry, I'm just looking for it here -- whether you know of Konstantin Kljajic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you tell us what Konstantin Kljajic was doing in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: For a while, he was at the command of the brigade before returning to the Ministry of Defence. I don't know exactly in which one of these two places he was at the time. I can't give you a precise answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, would I be right in saying that Konstantin Kljajic was at that time, in July of 1995, that he was actually a clerk in the personnel services of Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No, he was not. He was not an officer in the personnel service of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe there was a mistake in the translation. I didn't say "officer," I mentioned "clerk" in the personnel services of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, we did have a conversation with this person. Now, you say something different from what he told us, because he told us he was a clerk in Zvornik Brigade personnel services, but he also told us that you were in charge of all personnel activity relating to the mobilisation of soldiers and the admittance of recruits, as well as assignment. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: You are not right on that. In July 1995, in the section for personnel affairs, there was me and Andjelko Ivanovic. Bato, or rather Konstantin Kljajic, was a commanding officer who was with that section for a while before being sent to the staff office, but I don't remember the exact date of his transfer. I don't remember precisely and I cannot give you a precise answer to this question. Now, for the other part, that we admitted recruits and conscripts, and after serving their military service, these men would return and then they would be assigned to units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my question was not exactly that, but I will make it more precise. On both the 15th -- the 14th and the 15th of July, 1995, I suggest to you that as the person responsible for personnel, you had to be present to receive and assign new recruits, and that was strictly your obligation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: As far as responsibility, that could also have been done by the clerk for personnel, Andjelko Ivanovic or anyone else who was put in charge of that. It doesn't mean necessarily that only I was responsible for that. Andjelko Ivanovic or any other person authorised to perform that job could have done it and done it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Galic, you know who Stevan Ivanovic is; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And are you aware that he issued an order for mobilisation for July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we can have on e-court, please, document number 3D119. And we have it both in English and in B/C/S. And if I can have both side by side, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like you, Mr. Galic, to look at this document here and to read this, which is in your language. Now, there is of course a difference between the document in your language and the document which is in English, and I draw the attention of everyone in the courtroom to paragraph 3, which is circled, where in your language, Mr. Galic, it says that you are the point of contact, where it says: "Any unclear issues regarding mobilisation should be addressed to the Zvornik Brigade command," your name is there in your -- in the version in your language, but your name does not appear in the translation. Were you aware of this document, Mr. Galic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: This is a document I was not aware of, because it is addressed to the department of the Defence Ministry in Zvornik by the secretary of the Secretariat for National Defence. So there was no indication that this document should be addressed to the command of the Zvornik Brigade or the department for personnel. We can see here that it is to the Defence Ministry section of Zvornik, and then you will also see from the heading, if it could be scrolled down, please, you see here it says, "Republika Srpska, Ministry of Defence, Zvornik Department," which is superior to the Defence Ministry. So it is passed on from one to the other, and no mention is made here of the Zvornik Brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My question to you, Mr. Galic, is simply: I draw your attention to the paragraph which is right below where it says: "Ministry of Defence, Zvornik Department," and it says that this is based on a request which was made by Drina Corps command, but that's not what -- that's not my issue. The issue is: Are you telling this Court that you were not made aware that on 15 July there was supposed to be a mobilisation ordered by Mr. Ivanovic, the secretary?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I was aware of the mobilisation, the mobilisation of personnel who were part of the battalion, and on the 15th of July, as indicated in the order, it was mobilised. But I understood you to say that this was addressed to the brigade command, which it wasn't. It was addressed to the Defence Ministry that carried out these activities on the basis of orders from the Ministry or, rather, the Secretariat on the basis of the request of the Drina Corps commander of such-and-such a number. We received those people, and there's no question about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my next question, Mr. Galic, is: Are you aware -- or I simply suggest to you that knowing that there was mobilisation on that day, this must have been a major activity for you and your department some days before that.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I don't know what mobilisation before this. This is customary -- a customary activity of personnel who had been mobilised on several occasions, and this is carried out, and when the need for such a unit ceases, it is disbanded, but it is always ready, it is always available to be called up if necessary. The personnel in the unit from the work units who were working in companies, manufacturing, in various organisations that were still operating during the war, those were the people who were being called up. We called it the "R" battalion, the reserve battalion, and this order relates to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Galic, do you know how many people were mobilised on the 15th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact number, but this unit -- it's hard for me to engage in guesswork. I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to call up on the e-court document number 3D125, please. It's a document that is only available in the language of the witness, but it is a list of names and I think it should not cause too many problems. Mr. Galic, can you look at this document, and I will let you look at the first page, and then we can move straight to the last page. And will you agree with me, on the basis of this document, that 254 persons were mobilised on the 15th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: This is a list, and it confirms what I just said, that these were people from work organisations. This was the number that was called up. Whether they all responded or not, this is something I cannot recall and can't tell you. This is a list of the members of that unit that was on work duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if someone from Zvornik Brigade had any responsibility with these people to welcome them and then to send them away, that would be you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No. They are received by their commander, the commander of the unit. He's the person who does that. I am just the technical person who, with the help of the command that is being formed, is there to receive all those people and to register all data and inform the ministry who responded to the call-up, who did not, and all the other activities envisaged by law.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And on 14 and 15 of July, 1995, this Zvornik Brigade provided a gathering area for all these people?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: They gathered in the barracks. That was per -- that had its permanent security. It was never without security.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And were you there? Did you meet these people?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I was present. On the 15th, in the morning, I came from the forward command post. I went into the field for a while and came back. But I must draw attention to the fact that it is not my duty to receive each and every person, welcome him and assign him. It is the command who does all that. It is the command that informs the personnel department about the number of arrivals, and then this is monitored. Upon the completion of mobilisation, a list of those who failed to respond is provided to the Ministry of Defence to check out why they didn't respond and whether there is any grounds to institute proceedings because of their failure to respond to the call-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Galic, do you recall meeting these people on the 15th because I've just shown you a document or is that something that is live in your memory?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Well, I -- I do remember that people were gathering and leaving, but I really can't tell you much about the details that you're asking me to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Before I move on to my next topic, I would just like to come back quickly to your -- when you joined back the service in 1998. At what age did you join the service, and were you not past the normal age to join back?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1951, and I rejoined the service in 1998, so that was my age. And I was admitted into the service probably -- or certainly in accordance with all the regulations in force at the time, on the basis of which the ministry did admit people to professional military service of all categories.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And just my last question to close this topic: Did you not tell someone that Major Obrenovic, who was the commander at that time, did intercede in your favour because there was a problem with your age?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No, I never said that. That is not true. And it is not typical of me or Mr. Obrenovic. If I was beyond the age, I would have said, "Thank you," and gone to look for another honourable job, rather than doing this. Therefore, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on, Mr. Galic, to your interview with the investigator from the Prosecution. And would I be right in saying that when you met in 2001, you did mention that you had no involvement whatsoever in military action in July of 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you also explained to the investigator how is it that as the person responsible for personnel, you were immediately subordinated to the chief of staff? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall that you were shown an organisational chart by the investigator when you met him on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we can call up on e-court 3D120, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: While -- before we get this new exhibit on the -- or document on e-court, I'd ask you, Mr. Galic: You recognise the difference between someone who is an assistant commander within a unit for one of the departments and someone who, like you, is reporting directly to the Chief of staff; there is a difference, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: There is a difference. Could you please make it clearer, and could your questions be a little shorter, if possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will endeavour to make them shorter. What's the difference between an assistant commander and someone who reports directly to the chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. There's a lot of people that report to the chief of staff. If you could make that more specific, I think you'll get a better answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it would be fairer on the witness, too, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My pleasure to please my colleagues from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: How many assistant commanders were there in Zvornik Brigade in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Let us count them together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You've got the document in front of you. It shouldn't be too difficult.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Assistant commander for morale, religious and legal affairs, assistant commander for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I can't see anyone else from this chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Assistant commander for security, maybe?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: It says, "chief of security."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So the chief of security does not have the position of an assistant commander; is that what you're saying today?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: If I say that he is not, then according to this structure he should have a higher degree of responsibility and a higher position than any other assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what is the difference between someone like you, responsible for personnel, and someone who is either in the morale, in the logistics, or security departments or branches? What's the difference?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question. Neither was I assistant commander for morale, nor chief of security, nor assistant commander for logistics, so these are duties I cannot discuss. The only thing I can talk about is the assistant chief of staff for personnel, and I spent a certain amount of time during those -- doing those duties, so I can't make a distinction between what you are asking and the services I conducted. Every service has its weight, has its level of responsibility. What that is, I am not qualified or authorised to qualify the duties of the commander and the assistant commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me try and help you out, Mr. Galic. You, as chief of personnel, would report directly to Mr. Obrenovic, the chief of staff, whereas an assistant commander for morale, logistics or security would report directly to the commander. Does that ring any bell to you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: First of all, let me correct you. I wasn't the chief for personnel, but assistant chief of staff for personnel, so that is an important difference. I wasn't chief, but assistant. Now, the difference -- you see, I engaged in the activities I have described. The assistant commander for morale, for religious and legal affairs, as the title indicates, has responsibility for morale, for religious affairs and for legal affairs. Those are the three activities that that man united in his activities, as opposed to me, who had no involvement there. I did what I was told to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We'll leave it at that, but my next question is: When you were shown this organisational chart by the investigator, it was empty, was it not? There was no markings at all on it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No, you're not right. It was drawn out, but without the names, and I was asked if I -- as far as I can remember, to put down the names that I could remember and certain parts of units if certain units were left out. That was asked of me, and to the best of my recollection that is what I did at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And all these names that we find on this organisational chart were put there by yourself out of memory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Out of memory, I put down the names. I couldn't recollect the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we -- do you recall that you engaged into a discussion with the investigator, trying to explain to him what was the reserve battalion, because you noticed that there was something wrong there with the reserve battalion, who in your view is not part of the unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: This was a unit that was occasionally called up; it is not part of the establishment. It was called up according to the procedure that I have described.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you're not talking about those people who were mobilised when you talk about the reserve unit or the reserve battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you clarify? Are you saying that those people who were mobilised on the 15th and 14th of July, according to this document, that they are the members of the reserve battalion of the Zvornik Brigade? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. We'll move on to another topic. As the personnel officer or the assistant chief of staff for personnel, you did not have any contact with the commander, Vinko Pandurevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: In what period of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm referring, Mr. Galic, to July of 1995, specifically.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: On certain days, I did have contact, and on others, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in accomplishing your duties as the assistant chief of staff for personnel, who did you deal with most often, Obrenovic or the commander, Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I'm the direct inferior to Mr. Obrenovic, and according to the military hierarchy I'm also accountable to the commander of the brigade. But my immediate superior is the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to the period again in July of 1995, where you mentioned during your interview that from the 4th or the 5th of July until the 15th, that the commander, Pandurevic, was not there, and it was Major Obrenovic who was standing in for him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you also mentioned during that first interview that your first contact with the commander, Pandurevic, was on the 17th or the 18th of July, and that was because you did not leave your office at all during that period. Did you say that to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I said that in that period, that was the 17th or the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me call up the version of your interview just so that we can maybe help you out here, and I would like to have on e-court 3D115, which is the first interview with the investigator from the Prosecution. And I would like to go straight to page 9 in English and in B/C/S page 13. Now, I will read -- try to move ahead. I will read what you said on that occasion, and I quote from lines 7 to 12: "When he came back, you think, on the 15th, did you see him come back? "No. "How do you know he came back on that day? "I assume that because the unit that went with him also returned that day. "When was the first time that you spoke with Pandurevic or had dealings with him after he has returned? "I'm not so sure, but I think it was already after the 17th or the 18th, because they were in the field, and I did not leave the office at all during that period. I was not in contact with --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, could you check whether we have it in front of us?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, Judge. I will look. I thought we had the right one. What I'm looking for was 3D115. I don't think this is the one that is displayed now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It definitely isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I was looking for page -- in English, I was looking for page 9, and the number of the -- the tape interview is 69666. If we can go back a bit. I had page 9 also written on that document, but page 69666, four pages before that. And if I can have the equivalent in the language of the witness, please. No, there is a problem, Mr. President, because this is a mixed version with both English and -- this is a mixed version. This is not 3D115, unless --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now we have another page. Yes, I think we have it now. We have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: On the English channel is the good one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. We have it on the -- yes, we have it on the English channel as well here: "When was the first time you spoke with Pandurevic and had dealings with him after?" "I'm not sure, but I think --"

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Lines 10 to 12 is what I was referring the witness to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, one moment, Mr. Bourgon. Go ahead. Go ahead. Everything seems to be okay, Mr. Bourgon. You may proceed, unless you have a problem --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The document on the screen, on the e-court, is not the right document, so maybe there is something with the loading or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which document, in the original language or --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like both the original language and the English, if I could, for 3D115.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We have it for English, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay, so we have the -- I think maybe the wrong document was included in -- the scanned version is the mixed version with all languages. But on the left side --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Galic, I will simply read that quote again, and you can confirm that that was your answer. "When was the first time that you spoke with Pandurevic or had dealings with him after he has returned? "I'm not so sure, but I think it was already after the 17th or the 18th, because they were in the field, and I did not leave the office at all during that period, so I was not in contact with Pandurevic." Do you recognise these words in this interview?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: It's an interview in which I said I remembered it was around those dates. I didn't claim precisely that it was one way or another. I named the dates that I could remember, without having at my disposal any documents that would remind me of any details or that would give a precise indication of time and date when I met with the commander at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let's move on to -- unfortunately, it would be -- I'll try to get the right side with the same page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
